## Course Continuity Grounding

Groups 001 and 002 already laid the audit layer that this episode now uses as background. Group 001 established Chalmers's hard problem as the organizing challenge for phenomenal consciousness; separated phenomenal consciousness from access, reportability, wakefulness, metacognition, and behavioral control; warned that neural correlates can stand in many different relations to consciousness; and showed that worldview labels like physicalism, dualism, and idealism are starting points, not finished explanations. Group 002 added the primitive-or-not fork, the identity-demand audit, Kuhn's landscape as an organizing taxonomy, materialism as a research family rather than one theory, the brain-dependence evidence base, and the instability of non-reductive physicalism between identity and property dualism. [episodes/group-003/course_context.md; Kuhn 2024]

This dossier inherits those points. It does not restart the hard problem, redefine phenomenal versus access consciousness, reintroduce Kuhn's landscape as if new, re-explain materialism as one unified theory, or re-justify why neural correlates need a bridge relation. It does use those inherited distinctions when a section depends on them: the explanatory gap is invoked in panpsychism, monism, and dualism; the landscape framing is used to locate sections 11-15 in Kuhn's wider map; the identity-demand audit is used when monism and dualism cash out their dependence relations; and the brain-dependence base is used as the empirical pressure point against fundamental-consciousness, panpsychist, and dualist proposals. [course/episode_capsules/group-001.json; course/episode_capsules/group-002.json; course/callback_index.json]

The transition into group 003 is from the audit layer to a cluster of specific ontologies that try to answer it. Section 11 asks whether quantum physics plays a non-trivial role in phenomenal consciousness. Section 12 puts forward Integrated Information Theory as a consciousness-first identity proposal. Section 13 places experiential or proto-experiential character at the base of nature. Section 14 collects monist umbrella views that try to keep one world without either dualism's interaction gap or reductionism's explanatory gap. Section 15 returns to the option that consciousness needs a distinct ontological category. The cluster therefore stresses the same question from five different ontological angles. [Kuhn sections 11-15; data/research/11-15.json]

## Episode Scope And Why These Sections Are Grouped

This dossier covers Kuhn sections 11-15:

- Section 11: Quantum theories. Pages 61-61. Packet: `packets/theories/11-quantum-theories.md`
- Section 12: Integrated information theory. Pages 70-71. Packet: `packets/theories/12-integrated-information-theory.md`
- Section 13: Panpsychisms. Pages 73-73. Packet: `packets/theories/13-panpsychisms.md`
- Section 14: Monisms. Pages 77-77. Packet: `packets/theories/14-monisms.md`
- Section 15: Dualisms. Pages 83-83. Packet: `packets/theories/15-dualisms.md`

These five sections are grouped because they form the second ontological band of Kuhn's landscape after materialism and non-reductive physicalism. They share an explanatory ambition that goes beyond locating consciousness inside biological neural mechanism. Quantum theories propose that fundamental physics is doing non-trivial work. IIT proposes a specific identity claim from a consciousness-first axiomatic starting point. Panpsychism proposes that experience or proto-experience is already present in nature's basic furniture. Monism proposes that mental and physical are aspects, parts, or descriptions of one underlying reality. Dualism proposes that consciousness needs a distinct ontological category from the physical brain. The five do not form a single coherent rival to materialism; they are five different attempts to address what materialism appears to leave out, with very different epistemic statuses and very different mechanisms. [Kuhn sections 11-15; local packets 11-15]

## Concise Thesis Of The Cluster

The strongest thesis of this cluster is that no purely brain-mechanism account by itself fixes what consciousness is. Each section names a different way the brain-mechanism story might be incomplete: the wrong physics (section 11), the wrong level of description (section 12), the wrong starting ingredient (section 13), the wrong number of fundamental kinds (section 14), or the wrong number of ontological categories (section 15). Read together, the sections insist that any complete theory must say what consciousness is, not just what tracks, accompanies, measures, or reports it. [Kuhn 2024; Atmanspacher 2024; Tononi et al. 2016; Goff, Seager, & Allen-Hermanson 2022; Schaffer 2018; Robinson & Weir 2025]

The cluster's strongest case combines two pressures. First, the explanatory-gap pressure inherited from earlier episodes: structural, functional, and report-level descriptions do not transparently entail what experience is like. Second, an internal-fit pressure: each section claims to fit features that materialism handles awkwardly, including the apparent unity of experience, the difficulty of explaining qualitative character, the intrinsic-nature gap in physics, and the resistance of first-person identity to third-person redescription. [Levine 1983; Chalmers 2003; Tononi et al. 2016; Strawson 2006; Alter & Pereboom 2023; Swinburne 2013]

Where the cluster breaks is where each section must cash out the relation it claims to improve. Quantum theories must specify a non-trivial quantum variable that survives at biological scales and connects to phenomenal experience. IIT must defend the move from phenomenological axioms to physical postulates, the exclusion principle, and its anti-functionalist consequences. Panpsychism must answer the combination and decombination problems. Monism must say what the One is, why mental and physical descriptions both apply, and whether the proposal explains anything beyond the relabeling. Dualism must answer the interaction problem, the pairing problem, and the strong empirical record of brain dependence. The cluster is therefore an audit pass: each ontology offers a candidate fix for materialism's leftover problems and incurs its own. [Tegmark 2000; McKemmish et al. 2009; Doerig et al. 2019; Coleman 2014; Nagasawa 2021; Sider 2007; Kim 1989; Robb & Heil 2023]

## Per-Section Factual Summaries

### 11. Quantum Theories

Kuhn presents quantum theories of consciousness as a family claim. Quantum mechanics is supposed to play a necessary, specific role in generating phenomenal consciousness in brains or other physical systems, beyond the trivial fact that all matter is ultimately quantum. The family splits into three lines of work. Quantum brain theories look for literal quantum processes in neural tissue, as in Penrose and Hameroff's Orch OR, Stapp's mind-brain collapse framework, Beck and Eccles on quantum synaptic release, Vitiello and Freeman on quantum field models of brain dynamics, and Fisher's nuclear-spin proposal. Quantum mind or quantum cognition approaches use quantum probability, contextuality, complementarity, or non-commutative mathematics to model mental phenomena without claiming the brain is a quantum computer. Dual-aspect and Bohmian approaches, central to Pylkkanen's anchor text, use quantum theory to question classical assumptions about separability, mechanism, active information, and the mind-matter relation. [Atmanspacher 2024; Pylkkanen 2018; Hameroff & Penrose 2014; Fisher 2015; research record 11]

The strongest case is methodological rather than slogan-based. Some features of consciousness and cognition have tempted serious researchers to look beyond a purely classical-mechanistic picture: the unity and binding of experience, contextual shifts in thought, the apparent role of observation in quantum measurement, and the limits of current neural-correlate research. Quantum biology weakens a crude objection that warm, wet biology can never exploit quantum effects: photosynthesis, magnetoreception, and tunneling cases show that some biological systems may harness coherence or other non-trivial quantum features. Specific consciousness proposals also have the virtue of being at least partly falsifiable. Orch OR points to microtubules, anesthetic sensitivity, and objective reduction. Fisher's proposal points to phosphorus nuclear spins and Posner molecules. Chalmers and McQueen's consciousness-collapse work ties a quantified theory of consciousness to dynamical-collapse physics and possible quantum-computing tests. Pylkkanen's contribution is more philosophical: quantum theory forces theorists to inspect hidden classical assumptions about locality, separability, and mechanism. [Lambert et al. 2013; Hameroff & Penrose 2014; Fisher 2015; Chalmers & McQueen 2022; Pylkkanen 2018; Busemeyer & Bruza 2012]

The strongest objections are physical, biological, and explanatory. Relevance does not follow from fundamentality: quantum mechanics underlies chemistry and neurons, but that does not imply that quantum coherence, entanglement, or collapse is functionally relevant to cognition or phenomenal consciousness. Tegmark's decoherence calculation argues that candidate quantum degrees of freedom in the brain decohere far faster than ordinary neural processing times; Hagan, Hameroff, and Tuszynski disputed the estimate for microtubules, but the burden remains on proponents to identify protected quantum states in vivo. McKemmish, Reimers, McKenzie, Mark, and Hush argued that the original Orch OR picture does not fit known tubulin and microtubule chemistry; Reimers and coauthors later argued that the revised proposal is not scientifically justified. Fisher's nuclear-spin proposal is more disciplined but still speculative until Posner-molecule chemistry, spin coherence, neural readout, and behavioral consequences are demonstrated. Quantum cognition formalisms do not show quantum physics in the brain; they may be powerful probability models for order effects and contextual judgment while remaining compatible with classical neural implementation. Even confirmed long-lived quantum processes in neurons would still face the bridge problem: why would a wave-function collapse, microtubule coherence, or nuclear-spin entanglement feel like anything? Some quantum-consciousness literature also slides from precise physics into loose talk about universal mind, instantaneous synchrony, or spiritual holism; those versions are weakly evidenced unless they recover clear definitions and tests. [Tegmark 2000; Hagan, Hameroff, & Tuszynski 2002; McKemmish et al. 2009; Reimers et al. 2014; Carroll 2021; Kent 2021]

### 12. Integrated Information Theory

IIT claims that consciousness is identical to a system's maximally irreducible intrinsic cause-effect structure. It starts from phenomenology rather than behavior. Every experience exists for itself, is structured, is specific rather than generic, is unified rather than a bag of independent parts, and is definite in content and grain. IIT then translates these axioms into physical postulates about systems that can take and make a difference to themselves. A conscious system is therefore not merely a processor with the right input-output function. It must have the right intrinsic causal organization, quantified in principle by integrated information, usually called phi or Phi. The detailed geometry of that causal structure is supposed to specify the quality of experience. This is why IIT treats the cerebral cortex as a plausible substrate of ordinary human consciousness, the cerebellum as comparatively poor despite its many neurons, and a digital simulation of a brain as not automatically conscious unless the simulating hardware itself has the relevant intrinsic causal powers. [Tononi 2004; Balduzzi & Tononi 2009; Oizumi, Albantakis, & Tononi 2014; Tononi et al. 2016; Albantakis et al. 2023; research record 12]

The strongest case is that IIT attacks several central consciousness problems at once rather than treating consciousness as report, access, intelligence, or behavior. It gives a principled answer to why an experience is both differentiated and unified: a conscious state rules out many alternatives, yet does so as one irreducible whole. It explains why raw size or complexity is not enough, using the cortex-cerebellum contrast as its signature example. The theory also has unusual ambition about quality, not only level: qualia-space and IIT 3.0/4.0 aim to map the structure of experience to the structure of causal powers. Empirically, IIT has motivated useful measures of brain complexity such as the perturbational complexity index (PCI), which can distinguish wakefulness, dreamless sleep, anesthesia, locked-in syndrome, and some disorders of consciousness without relying on behavior. The 2025 Cogitate adversarial collaboration gave IIT partial empirical traction: the adversarial test found sustained conscious-content information in posterior cortex, although not all IIT predictions were supported. At its best, IIT is a rigorous consciousness-first research program with mathematical formalisms, clinical motivation, and partly testable neural predictions. [Tononi & Koch 2015; Casali et al. 2013; Casarotto et al. 2016; Cogitate Consortium 2025]

The strongest objections target IIT's foundations, measurement, and empirical status. Critics argue that the move from phenomenological axioms to physical postulates is not deductive: it may be a bold explanatory proposal but is not forced by introspection. The exclusion postulate in particular is often challenged as under-argued. Phi is extremely hard to compute for realistic systems, its formal definition has changed across versions, and practical measures such as PCI are inspired by integration and differentiation rather than direct measurements of IIT's full Phi-structure. IIT's anti-functionalist commitments create the sharpest philosophical pressure. If two systems have the same input-output behavior but different causal structure, IIT can say one is conscious and the other is not; the unfolding argument claims this makes causal-structure theories either false or empirically inaccessible. IIT also seems to attribute at least primitive experience to systems many researchers regard as plainly nonconscious, including some artificial circuits and networked artifacts; proponents may accept this as a revision of common sense, but critics see it as a sign that phi is tracking integration rather than consciousness. The 2025 Cogitate study did not find the sustained posterior synchronization IIT predicted, so empirical support is mixed. The newest IIT ontology goes beyond ordinary neuroscience by claiming that intrinsic entities are what truly exist and by deriving a strong view of free will; those metaphysical extensions are much less established than the clinical and neural complexity work. The 2023-2025 pseudoscience debate should be presented carefully: some critics argue IIT has outpaced its evidence and testability, while other non-IIT researchers argue that the pseudoscience label is too blunt for a theory that makes contact with experiments, formal modeling, and adversarial testing. [Cerullo 2015; Doerig et al. 2019; Merker, Williford, & Rudrauf 2022; IIT-Concerned et al. 2025; Gomez-Marin & Seth 2025]

### 13. Panpsychisms

Panpsychism is a family of views, not one settled theory. Kuhn's anchor presents its broadest claim: physical ultimates, whether particles, fields, energy-matter, or perhaps spacetime itself, have phenomenal or proto-phenomenal properties, so mentality is a primitive feature of reality rather than a late product of lifeless matter. Contemporary analytic panpsychists usually do not claim that electrons think, rocks feel pain, or quarks have beliefs. The serious versions more often claim that extremely simple experiential ingredients, proto-experiential ingredients, or intrinsic natures belong to fundamental physical reality and that animal consciousness appears only in organized aggregates under special conditions. Key variants include panexperientialism, panprotopsychism, constitutive micropsychism, emergentist panpsychism, Russellian panpsychism, cosmopsychism, and religious or cross-cultural forms such as Vedantic, Saiva, Buddhist, and Kabbalistic panpsychist or cosmopsychist readings. The central ambition is to keep consciousness inside nature while avoiding both reductive physicalism's explanatory gap and Cartesian dualism's interaction problem. [Kuhn 2024; Goff, Seager, & Allen-Hermanson 2022; Chalmers 2016; Strawson 2006; Goff 2017; research record 13]

The strongest case is a two-part metaphysical argument. First, the anti-emergence argument says that subjective experience is not intelligibly generated by rearranging purely nonexperiential structure and function. If consciousness is real and brute radical emergence is unsatisfying, it may be less ad hoc to suppose that experiential or proto-experiential character is already present in basic reality and becomes complex in organisms. Second, the Russellian intrinsic-nature argument says that physics tells us a great deal about mathematical, structural, causal, and dispositional relations but not the categorical nature of matter in itself. Consciousness is the one intrinsic nature we know directly from the inside, so panpsychism proposes that the hidden categorical nature of matter is at least partly consciousness-involving. Chalmers frames Russellian panpsychism as a possible synthesis: physicalism is attractive because of causal closure, dualism is attractive because it respects experience, and panpsychism tries to capture both by identifying phenomenal character with the intrinsic side of the physical. The best panpsychism is therefore not an anti-science doctrine. It accepts the public equations of physics, then adds a metaphysical interpretation of what their relata are intrinsically. Cross-cultural material, especially Vedantic and Saiva cosmopsychist traditions, broadens the menu of options by asking whether the fundamental conscious reality might be whole-first rather than particle-first. [Strawson 2006; Chalmers 2003; Alter & Pereboom 2023; Goff 2017; Maharaj 2020]

The strongest objections are severe. The combination problem asks how many micro-experiences or microsubjects could compose one unified human subject; subject-summing looks unlike ordinary physical composition, because putting many points of view near each other does not obviously create a new point of view. Cosmopsychism reverses the direction but inherits a decombination problem: how does one cosmic consciousness segment into many bounded finite subjects? Nagasawa argues that constitutive Russellian panpsychism reaches a cognitive dead end: even if it is true, we may be unable to specify what microphenomenal properties are or how they aggregate into macrophenomenal consciousness. A physics objection, pressed by Sean Carroll, is that if mental ultimates add new causal influences, they threaten well-tested physics; if they add no new influences, it is unclear what explanatory work they do. A methodological objection is that panpsychism has few distinctive empirical predictions and can look like relabeling the mystery rather than solving it. A boundary objection, associated in Kuhn's anchor with Searle, asks why consciousness comes in discrete subjects if mentality is spread through nature. Religious or mystical variants may be philosophically rich but should not be presented as scientific evidence for panpsychism; quantum-consciousness or cosmic-consciousness claims often slide from metaphysical interpretation to alleged physical proof. [Coleman 2014; Nagasawa 2021; Carroll 2021; Roelofs 2019; Goff, Seager, & Allen-Hermanson 2022]

### 14. Monisms

Kuhn's Monisms section is an umbrella category rather than a single testable mechanism. The anchor is Schaffer's metaphysical definition: monism attributes oneness to reality, and in the strict existence-monist form there is exactly one concrete object, with everything else identical to it or derivative from it. For consciousness theory, the relevant move is broader: whatever ultimately exists must include, ground, or express both what we call physical and what we call mental. That makes monism a crossroads between physicalism, panpsychism, neutral monism, Russellian monism, dual-aspect theories, idealism, anomalous monism, reflexive monism, and theological or spiritual one-reality views. The family resemblance is anti-Cartesian and anti-gap: do not put mind and matter into two fundamentally alien substances, and do not explain consciousness by simply omitting or deflating phenomenal experience. The price is that "monism" by itself is too thin. A serious monist theory must still say what the One is, how finite subjects arise within it, why mental and physical descriptions both apply, and whether the proposal adds explanatory power beyond relabeling the hard problem. [Schaffer 2018; Schaffer 2010; Alter & Pereboom 2023; Stubenberg & Wishon 2023; Atmanspacher 2012; Atmanspacher & Rickles 2022; Velmans 2008; research record 14]

The strongest case combines parsimony with integration. Substance dualism respects phenomenal consciousness but faces interaction, pairing, and causal-closure problems. Reductive materialism fits well with neuroscience but appears to leave an explanatory gap between complete structural, functional, or neural descriptions and what experience is like from the inside. Monist theories try to keep one world while avoiding both failures. Schaffer's priority monism gives the whole-first version: perhaps the cosmos is the one fundamental concrete object and parts are derivative, a view motivated by questions about quantum holism, atomless gunk, intrinsicness, and law-governed unity. Russellian monism gives the consciousness-focused version: physics tells us relational and dynamical structure, but not the intrinsic nature of the entities bearing that structure; consciousness is the one intrinsic reality we know directly, so phenomenal or protophenomenal properties may be the categorical base of physical reality. Neutral and dual-aspect monisms soften that claim by saying the underlying reality is neither simply mental nor simply physical, while mind and matter are two aspects, organizations, or descriptions of it. Davidson's anomalous monism offers a different, physical-ontology version: mental events are physical events, but psychological explanation is not reducible to strict physical law. At its best, monism is a disciplined attempt to make consciousness belong to nature without making nature merely third-person mechanism. [Schaffer 2010; Chalmers 2003; Alter & Pereboom 2023; Stubenberg & Wishon 2023; Davidson 1970; Yalowitz 2025; Atmanspacher & Rickles 2022]

The strongest objections start with category confusion. Monism about how many concrete objects are fundamental is not automatically a theory of consciousness; the claim that the cosmos is basic does not explain why there are pains, colors, thoughts, or unified subjects. Existence monism is especially hard to square with ordinary and scientific talk about many concrete things, while priority monism must defend controversial assumptions about dependence, fundamentality, and whether the whole really explains its parts. Consciousness-focused monisms have their own problems. Russellian and panpsychist versions face the combination problem: many micro- or proto-phenomenal ingredients do not obviously compose one bounded human point of view. Neutral monism must specify the neutral base without letting it collapse into disguised materialism, idealism, or dualism; otherwise "neutral stuff" becomes a placeholder. Dual-aspect monism can sound like a verbal truce unless it gives rules linking the two aspects and explains why brain changes track experience so tightly. Davidson's anomalous monism is vulnerable to the charge that mental properties become causally idle: if the event causes behavior only under its physical description, what causal work does mentality do? Physics-based objections press harder: if consciousness adds new causal influence, where does it enter tested physics; if it adds none, what explanatory work has been gained? Many spiritual, cosmic-mind, Jungian, or quantum-flavored monisms may be philosophically rich but become weakly evidenced when promoted as empirical science. Tegmark's "consciousness as a state of matter" proposal is a useful exemplar of formal monist physics that remains speculative until anchored to measurement and prediction. [Sider 2007; Coleman 2014; Kim 1989; Carroll 2021; Tegmark 2015]

### 15. Dualisms

Kuhn introduces dualism as the broad family of consciousness theories that posit at least two ontological categories: the physical brain and something mental or soul-like that is not identical with the physical world as currently conceived. In ordinary usage this usually means substance dualism: a person is, or includes essentially, a nonphysical mind or soul distinct from the body. Kuhn correctly separates this from property dualism, which may posit irreducible phenomenal properties without a separable soul. The key pressure point is causal. If the nonphysical mind affects speech, action, attention, or memory, then the physical world is not causally closed in the way many physicalists assume. If it does not affect the physical world, dualism risks epiphenomenalism, where consciousness is real but causally idle. The section should be framed less as one doctrine than as a decision tree: Cartesian substance dualism, soul-centered religious dualisms, hylomorphic and emergent dualisms, interactionism, epiphenomenalism, parallelism, and naturalistic dualism all preserve a mental/physical divide in different ways. [Kuhn 2024; Robinson & Weir 2025; research record 15]

The strongest case is not that neuroscience has failed but that third-person physical structure still seems to leave out first-person phenomenal character. Descartes gives the classical substance-dualist template: mind is essentially thinking and non-extended, body is extended and non-thinking, so they appear to be distinct kinds of substance. Plato's Phaedo supplies an older soul-centered version, tying personhood to a soul whose fate is not simply the body's fate. Contemporary arguments update the pressure. Chalmers's epistemic-gap framework argues that complete physical and functional facts do not transparently entail the existence of experience; Mary, zombies, Nagel's bat, and Levine's explanatory gap all push in the same direction. Swinburne's modern substance dualism adds a personal-identity argument: first-person identity and co-consciousness seem not to be captured by descriptions of a brain's parts, and it seems at least conceivable that the same subject could survive radical bodily or neural replacement. Interactionism also has a commonsense advantage: pain seems to make one withdraw, intentions seem to move bodies, and moral agency seems to require mental states to matter causally. A charitable formulation says dualism is trying to preserve three data at once: the reality of subjective experience, the unity and persistence of the subject, and the apparent causal role of deliberation and experience. [Descartes 1641; Plato Phaedo; Chalmers 2003; Swinburne 2013; Levine 1983]

The strongest objections are cumulative. The interaction problem, sharpened by Princess Elisabeth's challenge to Descartes, asks: if a soul is non-extended and not in physical contact with the body, what is the mind-body causal nexus? Contemporary versions appeal to conservation laws, the pairing problem, and the completeness or causal closure of the physical: if every bodily motion has a sufficient physical cause, a distinct nonphysical cause looks either excluded or systematically overdetermining. Dualism is also explanatorily expensive. It adds souls, psychophysical laws, or nonphysical substances without a worked-out mechanism for when they arise, how they attach to particular organisms, how they vary across species and development, or why brain injury, anesthesia, sleep, drugs, stimulation, and neurodegeneration alter consciousness so reliably. Dualism can trade one mystery for two: it leaves the hard problem in place and adds the problem of how an immaterial subject knows, unifies, remembers, and causes anything. Epiphenomenalist versions preserve causal closure but make experience causally irrelevant to reports about experience, which threatens knowledge of consciousness itself. Kuhn's survey gloss should be handled carefully: PhilPapers 2020 all-respondent figures show physicalism at 51.93% and non-physicalism at 32.08%, but PhilPapers warns these should not be used as a simple longitudinal comparison with 2009; the comparable-department analysis shows physicalism roughly stable or slightly higher. Soul-centered versions often depend on theological or spiritual premises. Those may be important culturally, but they are not independently confirmed by current neuroscience or physics. [Robinson & Weir 2025; Robb & Heil 2023; Papineau 2001; Koch et al. 2016; Bourget & Chalmers 2023]

## Strongest Academic Case For The Cluster

The best academic case for this cluster is not that one section wins, but that, taken together, they specify what materialism still owes and where its critics must do their own work.

First, the cluster shows that materialism's empirical leverage does not by itself answer the hard problem. The brain-dependence base established in group 002 constrains every section here, but section 11 asks whether classical neural mechanism is the right physics, section 12 asks whether information integration is the right level, section 13 asks whether the base ingredients of nature are right, section 14 asks whether the number of fundamental kinds is right, and section 15 asks whether the number of ontological categories is right. [Koch et al. 2016; Levine 1983; Kuhn 2024]

Second, the cluster contains the field's most disciplined consciousness-first research program. IIT begins from phenomenology, derives postulates, defines a measure, predicts a substrate, motivates a clinical index, and entered a 2025 adversarial test with risky predictions. Whether one accepts IIT or not, it shows that a consciousness-first theory can be made formal, partly testable, and clinically useful. [Tononi 2004; Tononi et al. 2016; Albantakis et al. 2023; Casali et al. 2013; Cogitate Consortium 2025]

Third, the cluster contains the strongest argument for the intrinsic-nature gap in physics. Russellian monism and Russellian panpsychism are not anti-physics; they accept the public equations and ask what occupies the structural roles. Even if false, this argument identifies a place where ordinary physicalism is silent and where consciousness is at least a candidate filler. [Strawson 2006; Chalmers 2003; Alter & Pereboom 2023; Goff 2017]

Fourth, the cluster reactivates whole-first metaphysics in a controlled way. Schaffer's priority monism and contemporary cosmopsychism are not slogans about cosmic mind; they articulate dependence relations that may better match quantum holism, atomless gunk, and law-governed unity than micro-first ontologies. [Schaffer 2010; Maharaj 2020]

Fifth, the cluster preserves the dualist option as a metaphysical response to phenomenal data and personal identity, not as anti-science nostalgia. Chalmers-style naturalistic property-level positions and Swinburne-style substance dualism are different proposals, and each puts genuine pressure on causal-closure assumptions even if neither wins on parsimony. [Chalmers 2003; Swinburne 2013]

Sixth, the cluster gives Kuhn's wide taxonomy real ontological content for the rest of the course. After group 003, the course can place quantum, IIT, panpsychist, monist, and dualist commitments on a single comparison grid and ask which combination of ontology, mechanism, and evidence each later theory claims. [Kuhn 2024; Seth & Bayne 2022]

## Serious Objections And Limits

- Fundamental physics matters to consciousness only if a proposal specifies a non-trivial quantum variable, shows it survives at the relevant biological scale and timescale, connects it to neural or cognitive organization, explains why it matters for phenomenal experience, and makes predictions not already delivered by ordinary neuroscience. [Tegmark 2000; Atmanspacher 2024]
- The original Orch OR proposal faces serious biological critique, and the revised proposal has been argued to be not scientifically justified; Fisher's nuclear-spin proposal remains a disciplined but unconfirmed hypothesis. [McKemmish et al. 2009; Reimers et al. 2014; Fisher 2015]
- Quantum cognition is a formal modeling program, not direct evidence that consciousness is generated by quantum brain physics. [Busemeyer & Bruza 2012]
- IIT's move from phenomenological axioms to physical postulates is not deductive, and the exclusion postulate, the change in Phi's definition across versions, and the gap between Phi and PCI all weaken the claim that current measurements verify the full identity claim. [Cerullo 2015; Merker, Williford, & Rudrauf 2022]
- IIT's anti-functionalist consequences are vulnerable to the unfolding argument, and the 2025 Cogitate result was mixed rather than confirmatory. [Doerig et al. 2019; Cogitate Consortium 2025]
- The 2023-2025 pseudoscience controversy should be presented as a methodological debate among serious researchers, not as a verdict. [IIT-Concerned et al. 2025; Gomez-Marin & Seth 2025]
- Panpsychism faces the combination problem, cosmopsychism faces a decombination problem, and Russellian panpsychism may reach a Nagasawa-style cognitive dead end. [Coleman 2014; Roelofs 2019; Nagasawa 2021]
- Panpsychist mental ultimates either add causal influence and threaten tested physics or add none and leave it unclear what they explain. [Carroll 2021]
- Monism about objects is not automatically a theory of consciousness, neutral monism risks placeholder bases, dual-aspect monism risks verbal truce, and anomalous monism risks causal idleness of the mental. [Sider 2007; Kim 1989; Stubenberg & Wishon 2023; Yalowitz 2025]
- Dualism must answer the interaction problem, the pairing problem, the strong empirical record of brain dependence, and the difficulty of specifying when and how souls or psychophysical laws attach to particular organisms. [Robinson & Weir 2025; Robb & Heil 2023; Papineau 2001; Koch et al. 2016]
- Soul-centered, cosmic-mind, divine-mind, Vedantic, Saiva, Buddhist, and Kabbalistic variants of panpsychism, monism, and dualism may be philosophically and culturally important, but they are not independently confirmed by current neuroscience or physics. [Maharaj 2020; Schipper 2021]

## Comparison Axes For Theories In This Cluster

- Ontological commitment: standard physical only; standard physical plus non-trivial quantum role; physical with intrinsic causal structure as identity base for consciousness; physical with intrinsic phenomenal or proto-phenomenal nature; one fundamental concrete reality with mental and physical aspects or descriptions; two fundamental kinds, substances, or categories.
- Identity relation for phenomenal consciousness: identical with a specific quantum process; identical with a maximally irreducible intrinsic cause-effect structure; grounded in micro-experiential or proto-experiential properties; grounded in cosmic consciousness; an aspect of a neutral or one-substance base; a distinct nonphysical substance or property.
- Relation to causal closure of the physical: respected (most monisms, IIT, quantum cognition, epiphenomenalist dualism); pressured (literal quantum-brain consciousness, interactionist dualism, panpsychist mental ultimates with added influence); accepted as open (some naturalistic dualisms and Russellian variants).
- Evidence base: empirically constrained neuroscience and clinical measures (IIT via PCI, brain-dependence base); formal mathematical modeling (quantum cognition, Phi/Φ, qualia space, Tegmark); speculative testable physics (Orch OR, Fisher, Chalmers-McQueen); analytic metaphysics (priority monism, Russellian monism, combination problem); historical and conceptual argument (Descartes, Plato, Phaedo).
- Stance on the combination/decombination problem: not central (most quantum-brain proposals, IIT); central and unresolved (constitutive micropsychism, Russellian panpsychism); central in reverse (cosmopsychism); avoided by claim (anomalous monism, dual-aspect monism); finessed by adding a substance (substance dualism).
- Stance on simulation and substrate: simulation is not duplication (IIT); substrate-neutral if the right physics is preserved (some quantum proposals); substrate is intrinsically experiential or proto-experiential (panpsychism, Russellian monism); substrate is one neutral base with two aspects (dual-aspect monism); substrate is irrelevant because the subject is nonphysical (substance dualism); substrate-dependent because consciousness is essentially biological (biological-naturalist variants in earlier sections).
- Failure modes specific to this cluster: relabeling mystery without mechanism; treating mathematical elegance as empirical confirmation; conflating quantum vocabulary with quantum physics; conflating monism about objects with a theory of consciousness; conflating cultural soul-talk with metaphysical proof; conflating panpsychist intrinsic-nature claims with established physics; conflating IIT's clinical indices with confirmation of its full identity claim.

## Epistemic Status And What Not To Overstate

Mainstream scientific status applies to quantum mechanics itself, to parts of quantum biology, to clinical measures inspired by IIT such as PCI, and to the strong empirical brain-dependence base. Mainstream scientific theory status applies to IIT as one of the leading contemporary consciousness theories with active mathematical, neuroscientific, and clinical work, even though its full identity claim and its 4.0 ontology remain controversial. [Lambert et al. 2013; Casali et al. 2013; Casarotto et al. 2016; Tononi et al. 2016; Albantakis et al. 2023; Koch et al. 2016]

Active philosophical debate applies to Russellian monism, Russellian panpsychism, panprotopsychism, constitutive micropsychism, emergentist panpsychism, cosmopsychism, priority monism, neutral monism, dual-aspect monism, anomalous monism, reflexive monism, substance dualism, hylomorphic dualism, property dualism, interactionism, parallelism, and naturalistic dualism. [Goff, Seager, & Allen-Hermanson 2022; Alter & Pereboom 2023; Schaffer 2018; Stubenberg & Wishon 2023; Yalowitz 2025; Robinson & Weir 2025]

Speculative extension applies to literal quantum-brain theories of phenomenal consciousness (Orch OR, Stapp, Beck-Eccles, Fisher), to consciousness-collapse interpretations, to whole-cosmos priority monism applied to consciousness, to Tegmark's consciousness-as-a-state-of-matter, and to naturalistic interactionist or property-dualist psychophysical laws. [Hameroff & Penrose 2014; Fisher 2015; Chalmers & McQueen 2022; Schaffer 2010; Tegmark 2015]

Religious or spiritual metaphysics applies to Vedantic, Saiva, Buddhist, and Kabbalistic panpsychist or cosmopsychist readings; to soul-centered substance dualisms tied to God, immortality, afterlife, or cosmic planes; to divine-mind, absolute-consciousness, or panentheistic monisms; and to spiritually purposive cosmic-mind readings of quantum theories. These can be philosophically rich and culturally important, but they are not independently confirmed by current neuroscience or physics. [Maharaj 2020; Schipper 2021]

Fringe or weakly evidenced claims include presenting quantum entanglement as proven mechanism for telepathy, brain-to-brain synchrony, or survival beyond death; presenting cosmic-mind monism as established physics; presenting panpsychism as having direct empirical measurements of micro-experience; and presenting substance dualism as scientifically confirmed by paranormal or near-death evidence. [Carroll 2021; Goff, Seager, & Allen-Hermanson 2022; Robinson & Weir 2025]

Do not overstate:

- Do not say quantum mechanics proves consciousness is quantum.
- Do not say quantum biology proves the brain is a quantum computer.
- Do not say quantum cognition shows quantum physics inside the brain.
- Do not say PCI directly measures IIT's full Phi-structure.
- Do not say the 2025 Cogitate adversarial collaboration confirmed IIT, or that it falsified IIT.
- Do not say the pseudoscience-IIT debate has been settled.
- Do not say panpsychism has empirical measurements of micro-experience.
- Do not say cosmopsychism has been independently established by physics.
- Do not say monism by itself solves the hard problem.
- Do not say priority monism follows directly from quantum holism.
- Do not say dual-aspect monism or anomalous monism delivers a mechanism for consciousness.
- Do not say PhilPapers' 2020 numbers track a clean trend from 2009.
- Do not say substance dualism has been disproved by neuroscience; do not say it has been confirmed by neuroscience.
- Do not say near-death or paranormal reports settle dualism.

## Implications Only Where Sources Justify Them

AI consciousness:

- Under IIT, an ordinary digital simulation of a brain is not automatically conscious because the simulating hardware may not have the right intrinsic causal powers; substrate matters. [Tononi et al. 2016; Albantakis et al. 2023]
- Under quantum-brain theories, AI consciousness depends on whether the relevant quantum process can be reproduced in artificial substrates; this is currently unsettled. [Atmanspacher 2024; Fisher 2015]
- Under panpsychism, all matter has some experiential or proto-experiential character, but only suitably organized systems may host unified subjects; the conditions remain underspecified. [Goff 2017; Coleman 2014]
- Under monism, AI consciousness depends on what the One is and how it gives rise to finite subjects, which is also underspecified. [Schaffer 2018]
- Under substance dualism, AI consciousness depends on whether a soul or nonphysical mind attaches to a system, which has no agreed criterion. [Robinson & Weir 2025]
- None of this group establishes that current AI systems are conscious.

Virtual immortality and mind uploading:

- IIT implies that a perfect software upload is not automatically conscious in the way the original brain is. [Tononi et al. 2016]
- Quantum-brain theories make uploading depend on whether the relevant quantum process is preserved. [Atmanspacher 2024]
- Panpsychism and Russellian monism do not by themselves favor uploading unless the upload preserves the relevant intrinsic-nature relations. [Strawson 2006; Alter & Pereboom 2023]
- Substance dualism is consistent with the soul's persistence independent of the brain, but offers no engineering route to preserve a particular subject in silicon. [Swinburne 2013]
- The cluster does not show that uploading preserves personal consciousness.

Survival beyond death:

- Brain dependence makes survival difficult for materialism, and the cluster's mainstream-science element preserves that pressure. [Koch et al. 2016]
- Substance dualism makes survival conceptually possible but supplies no independent empirical evidence for it. [Robinson & Weir 2025]
- Cosmopsychist and divine-mind monisms make some form of post-mortem continuation conceivable but, again, do not supply independent evidence. [Maharaj 2020]
- Survival as established empirical fact is not supported by anything in this cluster.

Meaning and value:

- IIT's claim that conscious experiences have intrinsic existence motivates some authors to ascribe moral status by Phi-related grounds; this is a contested extension. [Tononi et al. 2016]
- Dualism and soul-based metaphysics often ground objective meaning in the soul's nature or destiny, but as a metaphysical commitment rather than a neuroscientific finding. [Swinburne 2013]
- The cluster supplies only conditional implications for meaning and value, not a settled answer.
